tagline: A trading route became a highway through salmon and eagle country.
intro: The Haines Highway follows the Chilkat River through coastal rain forest toward the Canadian border. FHWA lists this Alaska National Scenic Byway as 44 miles, allowing one hour, and emphasizes its passage through eagle feeding and roosting grounds. The wider highway continues through British Columbia to Haines Junction in Yukon. The longer drive climbs into the St. Elias Mountains and Canada, where coastal forest gives way to alpine tundra.

Chilkat Tlingit traders used the earlier trail, later known as the Dalton Trail; some Klondike prospectors followed it in 1898 and 1899. In 1943, the U.S. Army built the highway as an alternative connection from the Pacific to the Alaska Highway if the White Pass and Yukon Route railway was blocked. After the war, blizzards and summer mudslides complicated travel, and maintenance was uneven. Year-round access followed in 1963. Complaints over road conditions led to the congressionally funded Shakwak reconstruction project, begun in 1976, covering this highway and part of the Alaska Highway.

Leaving Haines, the drive reaches eagle-viewing country at highway miles 12 to 18, then Klukwan on the Chilkat River. Farther along, the road runs through the Klehini River valley; Porcupine lies across that river near Mile 35. The Alaska journey ends at the Dalton Cache–Pleasant Camp border crossing.

moments.title: Alaska Chilkat Bald Eagle Preserve
moments.text: Late salmon runs bring eagles to the Chilkat River after summer has passed. Alaska DOT describes hundreds roosting in roadside cottonwoods between October and January. The state established the preserve in 1982. It extends mainly along the Chilkat, with sections on the Klehini and Tsirku rivers. Highway miles 12 to 18 are a popular viewing stretch. The gathering is seasonal, but eagles also live in the preserve year-round: its Wikipedia account gives a resident population of 200 to 400 birds. The seasonal feeding grounds are part of the byway itself, with the highway passing through the preserve beside the river.
moments.notice: Between October and January, look for eagles roosting in the cottonwoods beside the highway.

moments.title: Klukwan
moments.text: Klukwan is home to the Chilkat Indian Village, a federally recognized tribe headquartered here. The village stands on the north side of the Chilkat River, 21 miles northwest of Haines. It began along the trading route later known as the Dalton Trail. Wikipedia gives its Tlingit name as Tlakw Áan, meaning roughly “forever village,” a reference to its antiquity. The same account identifies Klukwan as the only remaining one of five Chilkat villages that existed in the area before 1900. Near the village, the glacier-fed Tsirku River ends in a delta four miles wide.

moments.title: Porcupine
moments.text: Gold found along Porcupine Creek in 1898 brought a seasonal mining community into being. Porcupine lies across the Klehini River, about a mile southwest of highway Mile 35. With a transient population, permanent buildings accumulated gradually. When the district entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1976, about 25 structures remained in varying states of decay. Most dated from 1927 to 1936, when the Sunshine Mining Company was the largest operator in the area.
